context.in_practice: Route 1 adds tests that run many random sequences of `config set` against generated files. The files vary in line endings (LF and CRLF), use both inline and indented YAML-style layouts, and include other files. After each save the test checks that the value reads back exactly and that a CRLF file has no lone LF line breaks. The tests are seeded, so a failure can be replayed, and no new library is needed. Route 2 adds no randomised testing, so write-back is checked only by the hand-written cases that already exist. Odd combinations nobody thought to write a test for stay unchecked until a user hits them.
context.stakes: If saving a setting ever corrupts the config file, users lose settings or end up with a broken file. Examples include a value that doesn't read back the same, or a Windows-style (CRLF) file that ends up with mixed line endings. Rare file shapes are where this tends to hide.
context.tradeoff: Route 1 costs extra test code, longer test runs, and occasional failures that take effort to shrink to a minimal case. Route 2 costs nothing now but leaves rare write-back bugs to be found by users.

plan_why: The question is about how the write-back was tested (seeded random or property tests versus none), which is test structure with no CLI behaviour of its own. Any CRLF or read-back bug these tests might have caught would depend on the individual implementation and could not be traced back to the testing route, so no command can show what each route results in.
routes: Random set sequences or seeded property tests over LF/CRLF, flow, block and includes, with no new dependency
